What is missing: a persistent, broader entry point - e.g. surfacing paths already known to be locked from a failed purge/uninstall attempt, or a quick-pick list of the current app's own leftover items mid-wizard, rather than only the single post-purge shortcut.

Needs its own design pass: where does the 'known locked items' list come from (recent failed purges via oplog? the current wizard's leftover tree specifically?), and how does that avoid becoming yet another list the operator has to maintain.

title: Windows Update: a legible list and a one-click handoff, not a rollback engine
description:
UN-CUT and rescoped 2026-08-12. I cut this as redundant; the operator corrected the premise and they are right: Windows CAN roll updates back, but the process and interface are hostile - Settings > Windows Update > Update history > Uninstall updates, several clicks deep, a bare KB list with no indication of what any of them is, no install dates surfaced usefully, and no explanation of what removing one costs you.

So the redundancy was never the rollback - it was ME proposing to reimplement wusa/DISM. That part stays cut. What we build is the part Windows does badly:

BUILD (ours, and small):
  - A legible list. Get-HotFix + DISM /Online /Get-Packages, both READ-ONLY, joined into one view: KB number, what kind of update it is (security / cumulative / driver / .NET), when it was installed, and whether it is removable at all (many cumulative updates are not, and Windows tells you this only by failing).
  - The one piece of judgement nobody offers: 'installed 3 days ago' next to 'this machine started misbehaving 3 days ago'. That is the actual reason anyone opens this screen, and it is the same question zrw's snapshot diff answers for installers. Cross-reference the two once both exist.
  - An honest cost line per update, especially for security updates.

DO NOT BUILD (this is the redundant half, still cut):
  - No removal engine. The Remove button shells out to the Windows mechanism that already exists and lets IT do the work and own the outcome: wusa.exe /uninstall /kb:NNNNNNN for MSU-packaged updates (which shows Windows' own uninstall UI and its own restart prompt), or open Settings' Uninstall Updates page directly (ms-settings:windowsupdate-history) when the package is CBS-only and wusa cannot take it.
  - No vault entry, no restore manifest, no progress UI of our own. We do not own this removal and must not imply we can reverse it - Windows Update reinstalls the update, that is the restore path, and the UI should say exactly that.
  - No auto-selection, no 'clean up old updates' bulk action, ever.

This is the same shape as the native-uninstaller handoff the wizard already does: Vanish finds it, explains it, and lets the vendor's own tool perform the destructive act.

Rule note: MANDATORY-REVIEW-GATE still applies, and is trivially satisfied because the user ends up in Windows' own confirmation UI.
design: Read-only until the handoff. The entire feature is a query, a join, and a ShellExecute - if it grows a removal code path of its own, it has become the thing we cut.
acceptance_criteria: Every listed update shows type, install date and removability; the Remove action launches the Windows mechanism rather than performing the removal; nothing in the UI claims Vanish can restore an update it did not remove.
notes: PARKED 2026-08-06 by operator directive ('implode the fluff, build a robust software'). This stage was scoped during a session that added new roadmap surface while the ALREADY-SHIPPED surfaces were substantially broken (see epic vanish-uninstaller-7oo). Scoping was sound; the sequencing was not. Do not start this until epic 7oo's P0 children are closed against real data. Rule 16's Core-VM gate still applies on top of that.

title: Stage 16: Orphaned Firewall Rule sweep
description:
Standard-tier feature, scoped 2026-08-05 while expanding what Vanish sees/lists/rectifies. Full spec: docs/roadmap.md Stage 16.

Distinct from the Firewall Controller cut from Stage 7 -- that was about judging live processes as 'suspicious' (Rule 6 boundary, still cut, unchanged). This is pure path-existence: does the program a firewall rule references still exist on disk. Same orphan-detection pattern already used for SharedDLLs (Stage 11) and fonts (Stage 12).

Measured on the operator's machine 2026-08-05: 659 total firewall rules, 48 reference a program path that no longer exists once environment variables are expanded. First measurement pass got this wrong -- Test-Path doesn't expand %SystemRoot%-style variables and flagged 295 false positives against live Windows system binaries before being corrected. The real 48 split into dead OS-feature rules (Windows Media Center's ehome\*, removed from Windows years ago; P2P Collaboration Foundation, deprecated), a temp installer's leftover rule, and rules pointing at a since-moved/uninstalled third-party app.

Implementation: Get-NetFirewallRule + Get-NetFirewallApplicationFilter, [Environment]::ExpandEnvironmentVariables on the Program path, then Test-Path. Quarantine-first per Rule 2 (export before removal, not a bare Remove-NetFirewallRule). Per Rule 24, label each finding by why it's dead (removed OS feature / uninstalled third-party app / leftover installer temp path), not a bare 'orphaned' list. Needs elevation for the write path; read/list can run in Audit Mode.

Blocked on: Core tier VM-tested (Rule 16) before it can release, same as every other Standard-tier stage -- design/implementation work is not blocked, only shipping is.

Also considered and rejected in the same pass: UWP/MSIX leftover package-data audit (Packages folders with no matching installed AppxPackage). Measured 14 of 144 folders orphaned, only 25.4MB total, one real item over 1MB. Not worth a dedicated feature at this size -- LEAVE-ALONE per Stage 14's tiering principle, re-measure later if it ever shows up bigger.
acceptance_criteria: Scan lists firewall rules whose Program path fails Test-Path after environment-variable expansion, each labeled with a plain-language reason (removed OS feature / uninstalled app / leftover installer). A planted orphaned rule (fake program path) is found, quarantined (exported before removal), removed, and restored from the vault; restore is verified by the rule reappearing in Get-NetFirewallRule. No removal path exists without a restore/export step.
notes: Kept as a cheap finding type on the existing scan surface, demoted to P3. Nothing else does firewall-rule orphan detection, so it is not redundant - but it frees ZERO disk space and fixes no user-visible symptom (48 dead rules of 659 measured). Ship it when the scan surface is already open, never as its own project.

title: Stage 15: Bandwidth diagnostics panel + Game/Stream Mode toggle
description:
Standard-tier feature, scoped 2026-08-05 from the Stage 7 disposition after the operator asked for network oversight to keep gaming/streaming from getting starved. Full spec: docs/roadmap.md Stage 15.

Scope boundary (binding, not just current-phase): no real-time per-app packet-level QoS -- that needs a kernel-mode WFP callout driver, a categorically different risk class than anything else in this codebase (driver signing, BSOD blast radius, new privileged attack surface). Permanently out of scope, not deferred. Also cannot fix LAN-level contention from another device -- that's a router problem, out of this app's reach; the panel should say so rather than imply otherwise.

Two parts:
1. Bandwidth panel (read-only): Get-NetTCPConnection/Get-NetUDPEndpoint grouped by OwningProcess, cross-referenced to Get-Process, remote address resolved best-effort. System-wide throughput from Get-NetAdapterStatistics deltas. Per Rule 9, ships as active-connections + system-wide throughput only -- true per-process byte-rate needs an ETW consumer, that is a separate, separately-justified v2.
2. Game/Stream Mode toggle: operator manually picks the process(es) to prioritize (no auto-detect heuristic for v1, matches Stage 4's manual-input philosophy). On enable: throttle Delivery Optimization, throttle/pause BITS, raise selected process priority class, tag selected traffic via New-NetQosPolicy DSCP marking (documented as router/ISP-dependent, no guarantee). On disable: revert every setting touched, same schema-rule-5 pattern as startupMode.

Explicitly cut, not part of this issue: Firewall Controller and general per-app Network Inspector (IP resolution as a security surface) -- Rule 6 boundary, unchanged.

Blocked on: Core tier VM-tested (Rule 16) before it can release, same as every other Standard-tier stage -- design/implementation work is not blocked, only shipping is.
design:
THREE MODELS (operator review 2026-08-07). Bandwidth is a volume problem, ping is a queue problem; conflating them is why network optimizers have their reputation. The biggest lever for ping is the same lever as for bandwidth - your own background traffic is usually your own bufferbloat - so this is one set of levers described honestly twice, not two features.

MODEL A, secure bandwidth. Answers 'my download crawls when Windows is busy'. Levers: pause BITS, cap Delivery Optimization, suspend named consumers, hold until switched off. Says: 'Windows Update paused. 3 transfers held. Nothing else changed.' Cannot give an app more than the link carries - it clears the lane, it does not widen the road. DECISIVE: the actions conclusively remove a competitor and the effect is observable in adapter throughput.

MODEL B, protect ping. Answers 'my game spikes when someone else streams'. Levers: stop this PC filling the queue, DSCP-mark the chosen app, disable NIC power saving, say when Wi-Fi is the cause. Says: 'This PC is no longer adding to the queue. Spikes left are not from here.' Cannot touch another device's traffic - that queue is in the router. NOT DECISIVE: DSCP only helps if the path honours it, and the dominant cause is often a device Vanish cannot see. So A reports what it DID; B reports what it RULED OUT.

MODEL C, best available. Both sets applied together, observed before/during/after, every setting reverted on exit, and it names what it could not reach. Cannot promise a number.

FOURTH OUTCOME, the one nobody ships: any model may end in 'nothing on this machine is the problem'. Say that plainly, show what was examined, point at router QoS - instead of applying five settings and implying they helped.

MEASUREMENT, and how it lands on INV-4: Model A needs throughput only (Get-NetAdapterStatistics deltas) - local, free, no network I/O, no invariant touched. Model B needs RTT under load vs idle, and the cheapest honest source is the DEFAULT GATEWAY: stays on the LAN, contacts no third party. By the letter of INV-4 that is still runtime network I/O, so it is an operator decision, not something to slip in - but it is categorically different from calling speedtest.net.

BUILD ORDER: (1) attribution panel, no network I/O, useful alone; (2) suppression + guaranteed full revert - the real value and the testable part; (3) latency diagnosis, only with the gateway-RTT carve-out approved; (4) DSCP marking last, labelled conditional because it may do nothing.

COPY RULE, testable: the panel states what it changed and what it observed, and never states a delta as a causal claim. A test can fail any percentage-improvement string in this surface, the same way the copy tests assert intent rather than exact prose. Banned: 'up to 40% faster', 'connection grade B+', 'optimized for gaming', 'ping improved by 22ms', 'boost enabled'.
acceptance_criteria: Bandwidth panel lists active TCP/UDP connections grouped by owning process with resolved remote host and system-wide adapter throughput -- no per-process byte-rate claimed. Game/Stream Mode toggle: operator selects target process(es), enabling throttles Delivery Optimization + BITS, raises target priority class, and applies a DSCP QoS policy; disabling reverts every one of those settings back to its prior state, verified by a settings round-trip test. No kernel driver, no per-app real-time packet shaping, no firewall control, no per-app IP/threat display shipped under this issue.
notes: NARROWED 2026-08-12. The read-only bandwidth panel is redundant - Task Manager and Resource Monitor both show per-process network already, and Vanish's own Network Activity panel (bfh.1, shipped) covers attribution. Cut that half. The part nobody else offers is the HOLD (bfh.2): pausing background transfers with a guaranteed way back. bfh.2 is already built and only needs its elevated confirmation, so this parent should not carry panel-expansion scope any more.

title: TASK-16: Multi-user hive sweep + ownership elevator (SHOULD)
description: Phase 4. Full spec: docs/planning/05-implementation-plan.md TASK-16 (context manifest, steps, verify, done-when). Read ONLY the context manifest listed there. Deviation protocol binding.
close_reason: TASK-16 partially done (SHOULD). REQ-17 multi-user profile sweep implemented: enumerates ProfileList, skips the current user, service accounts and already-loaded hives, reg-loads each inactive NTUSER.DAT under HKU\VanishProfile_*, scans Software for a caller-supplied keyword, and unloads every mounted hive in a finally with a GC flush first (NFR-07). Requires a keyword by design - without one it proposes nothing rather than listing every vendor key. Verified elevated via test/phase4-verify.ps1: no hive mounted before, none left mounted after, including on the empty-keyword path. REQ-19 ownership elevator is implemented in the engine (Grant-VanishOwnership: takeown + icacls to Administrators, invoked per item only when the caller passes allowOwnershipElevation and the move failed with an access error, recorded as aclElevated in the manifest row) but is NOT yet surfaced in the wizard UI as a per-item offer, and its acceptance test (quarantining a TrustedInstaller-owned file) has NOT been run. Filing that remainder as its own issue rather than claiming it.

title: TASK-09: Watchdog suspension (SHOULD, blocked on OPEN-01)
description: Phase 2. Full spec: docs/planning/05-implementation-plan.md TASK-09 (context manifest, steps, verify, done-when). Read ONLY the context manifest listed there. Deviation protocol binding.
close_reason: TASK-09 done (SHOULD, delivered): NtSuspendProcess/NtResumeProcess via Add-Type per OPEN-01, process tree discovered through Win32_Process BFS, handles held open from discovery through the whole freeze so a recycled PID cannot be resumed or killed by mistake. ProcessFreezer implements IDisposable and Unlock-Path calls Dispose() in a finally, so the thaw is guaranteed including on error. Terminate() resumes before terminating. Verified elevated via test/phase2-verify.ps1 with a real watchdog pair: CONTROL case proves killing the holder alone lets the watchdog respawn it; the suspend-then-unlock path leaves the file free with no respawn; and no test process is left suspended afterwards. Undocumented ntdll export retained deliberately per OPEN-01 - do not 'fix' it back to SuspendThread.

comments.author: QuantumMonkey
comments.text:
OPEN-01 FINDINGS (Gemini Pro, 2026-07-11):
Recommended mechanism: NtSuspendProcess/NtResumeProcess (ntdll), process tree discovery via Get-CimInstance Win32_Process.
Why: undocumented but the exact API Sysinternals Process Explorer uses; stable across Win10/11; atomic kernel-level whole-process suspension. Documented SuspendThread+Toolhelp32 alternative has a TOCTOU race (threads spawn during enumeration).
Code sketch: scratch/NtSuspendProcess-Sketch.ps1 (Antigravity scratch - NOT merged; Sonnet reimplements per spec gate).
Failure modes: Access Denied on protected/higher-priv processes (mitigated: Vanish runs elevated); PID reuse during discovery (mitigated: hold handles open after discovery).
Resume guarantee: C# class implements IDisposable storing opened handles; PS wraps in try/finally { $suspender.Dispose() } so resume+handle-close always runs.
Confidence 9/10; residual risk = MS deprecating the ntdll export (improbable - would break debuggers/anti-cheat/security tooling).

title: About page: decide whether to keep full tech-stack + data-folder-path disclosure
description: renderer.js:1052-1079 About panel reveals exact Electron/Chromium/Node versions, GitHub repo URL, and the full local Data folder filesystem path (info.dataDir) verbatim. Open product question, not a bug: does full version disclosure or the raw local path create any downside for an open-source, no-network desktop tool? Record the decision and reasoning (likely: keep -- no network exposure, matches project's transparency ethos -- but consider making the data-folder line a 'reveal in Explorer' action instead of raw text) rather than changing silently.
close_reason: Decision: keep full tech-stack + data-folder disclosure on About. Reasoning: Vanish has zero network I/O (asserted by test/network-verify.ps1), so exact Electron/Chromium/Node versions and the local data-folder path are never exposed to anyone but the person already sitting at the machine looking at its own About panel - there is no remote attacker this could inform. Matches the project's stated transparency ethos ('never pretends it can do something it cannot'). Not changed: the data-folder line could become a clickable 'reveal in Explorer' action to match Settings' existing set-open-data button, but that is a UX nicety, not a disclosure-risk fix - left for a future pass, not bundled into this one.

title: Stage 10 (Extended): WMI/DCOM orphans, event log channels, offsets DB
description: Extended tier, no committed timeline, no issue until now. DCOM/WMI namespace cleanup carries promptgate Rule 17: mandatory per-item review gate, auto-deletion permanently disabled by default, quarantine manifest before any removal. Also here: orphaned EventLog channel registrations, and the crowdsourced offsets JSON for mapping atypical directories (.config, .toolcache, .unity3d) that do not match application names. Waits on the clean-VM pass (0xt) like everything else Standard-and-above.
close_reason:
Cut as redundant, per operator direction 2026-08-12: 'solve problems that are not solved... dont build redundant nonsense'.

ag0 (Windows Update rollback): Windows Settings > Installed Updates already does this, using the EXACT mechanisms this issue specified - wusa.exe /uninstall and DISM /Remove-Package. Vanish would be a second front-end on the same API with no added capability: the vault cannot make a removed security update reversible in any way Windows' own reinstall does not already, and the issue's own binding requirement (MANDATORY-REVIEW-GATE, no auto tier) means it cannot even be faster. The genuinely unserved question nearby is 'which update correlates with when this machine changed', which is zrw's snapshot diff, not a rollback button.

0ng (Driver Store sweeper): pnputil ships with Windows and Disk Cleanup already offers 'Device driver packages'. Worse, the issue documents that INV-1 CANNOT be honoured here - pnputil /delete-driver destroys the FileRepository copy, so a restore manifest would be a promise the vault cannot keep. Building a removal path that breaks the app's own foundational invariant to duplicate a built-in tool is the definition of what we are cutting. The audit-only half already ships (cleaner-scan cleaner=drivers, removable=false) and is the honest version.

dfe (WMI/DCOM orphans, event log channels, offsets DB): P4, no committed timeline, near-zero user-visible value, and Rule 17 would gate it behind mandatory per-item review anyway. Nothing here is a problem a user has ever reported having.

None of these are deleted work - each is recoverable from bd history if the reasoning changes.
